### The Same Conclusion Supported by the Transfiguration. Marcion Inconsistent in Associating with Christ in Glory Two Such Eminent Servants of the Creator as Moses and Elijah. St. Peter's Ignorance Accounted for on Montanist Principle.

Chapter XXII.—The Same Conclusion Supported by the Transfiguration. Marcion Inconsistent in Associating with Christ in Glory Two Such Eminent Servants of the Creator as Moses and Elijah. St. Peter’s Ignorance Accounted for on Montanist Principle.

You ought to be very much ashamed of yourself on this account too, for permitting him to appear on the retired mountain in the company of Moses and Elias,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4319] whom he had come to destroy. This, to be sure,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4320] was what he wished to be understood as the meaning of that voice from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, hear Him”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4321]—*Him*, that is, not Moses or Elias any longer. The voice alone, therefore, was enough, without the display of Moses and Elias; for, by expressly mentioning whom they were to hear, he must have forbidden all[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4322] others from being heard. Or else, did he mean that Isaiah and Jeremiah and the others whom he did not exhibit were to be heard, since he prohibited those whom he did display? Now, even if their presence was necessary, they surely should not be represented as conversing together, which is a sign of familiarity; nor as associated in glory with him, for this indicates respect and graciousness; but they should be shown in some slough[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4323] as a sure token of their ruin, or even in that darkness of the Creator which Christ was sent to disperse, far removed from the glory of Him who was about to sever their words and writings from His gospel. This, then, is the way[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4324] how he demonstrates them to be aliens,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4325] even by keeping them in his own company! This is how he shows they ought to be relinquished: he associates them with himself instead! This is how he destroys them: he irradiates them with his glory! How would their own Christ act? I suppose He would have imitated the frowardness (of heresy),[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4326] and revealed them just as Marcion’s Christ was bound to do, or at least as having with Him any others rather than His own prophets! But what could so well befit the Creator’s Christ, as to manifest Him in the company of His own foreannouncers?[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4327]—to let Him be seen with those to whom He had appeared in revelations?—to let Him be speaking with those who had spoken of Him?—to share His glory with those by whom He used to be called the Lord of glory; even with those chief servants of His, one of whom was once the moulder[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4328] of His people, the other afterwards the reformer[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4329] thereof; one the initiator of the Old Testament, the other the consummator[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4330] of the New? Well therefore does Peter, when recognizing the companions of his Christ in their indissoluble connection with Him, suggest an expedient: “It is good for us to be here” (good: that evidently means to be where Moses and Elias are); “and let us make three tabernacles, one for Thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias. But he knew not what he said.”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4331] How knew not? Was his ignorance the result of simple error? Or was it on the principle which we maintain[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4332] in the cause of the new prophecy,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4333] that to grace ecstasy or rapture[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4334] is incident. For when a man is rapt in the Spirit, especially when he beholds the glory of God, or when God speaks through him, he necessarily loses his sensation,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4335] because he is overshadowed with the power of God,—a point concerning which there is a question between us and the carnally-minded.[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4336] Now, it is no difficult matter to prove the rapture[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4337] of Peter. For how could he have known Moses and Elias, except (by being) in the Spirit? People could not have had their images, or statues, or likenesses; for that the law forbade. How, if it were not that he had seen them in the Spirit? And therefore, because it was in the Spirit that he had now spoken, and not in his natural senses, he could not know what he had said. But if, on the other hand,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4338] he was thus ignorant, because he erroneously supposed that (Jesus) was their Christ, it is then evident that Peter, when previously asked by Christ, “Whom they thought Him to be,” meant the Creator’s Christ, when he answered, “Thou art the Christ;” because if he had been then aware that He belonged to the rival god, he would not have made a mistake here. But if he was in error here because of his previous erroneous opinion,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4339] then you may be sure that up to that very day no new divinity had been revealed by Christ, and that Peter had so far made no mistake, because hitherto Christ had revealed nothing of the kind; and that Christ accordingly was not to be regarded as belonging to any other than the Creator, whose entire dispensation[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4340] he, in fact, here described. He selects from His disciples three witnesses of the impending vision and voice. And this is just the way of the Creator. “In the mouth of three witnesses,” says He, “shall every word be established.”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4341] He withdraws to a mountain. In the nature of the place I see much meaning. For the Creator had originally formed His ancient people on a mountain both with visible glory and His voice. It was only right that the New Testament should be attested[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4342] on such an elevated spot[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4343] as that whereon the Old Testament had been composed;[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4344] under a like covering of cloud also, which nobody will doubt, was condensed out of the Creator’s air. Unless, indeed, he[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4345] had brought down his own clouds thither, because he had himself forced his way through the Creator’s heaven;[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4346] or else it was only a precarious cloud,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4347] as it were, of the Creator which he used. On the present (as also on the former)[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4348] occasion, therefore, the cloud was not silent; but there was the accustomed voice from heaven, and the Father’s testimony to the Son; precisely as in the first Psalm He had said, “Thou art my Son, today have I begotten thee.”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4349] By the mouth of Isaiah also He had asked concerning Him, “Who is there among you that feareth God? Let him hear the voice of His Son.”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4350] When therefore He here presents Him with the words, “This is my (beloved) Son,” this clause is of course understood, “whom I have promised.” For if He once promised, and then afterwards says, “This is He,” it is suitable conduct for one who accomplishes His purpose[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4351] that He should utter His voice in proof of the promise which He had formerly made; but unsuitable in one who is amenable to the retort, Can you, indeed, have a right to say, “This is my son,” concerning whom you have given us no previous information,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4352] any more than you have favoured us with a revelation about your own prior existence? “Hear ye Him,” therefore, whom from the beginning (the Creator) had declared entitled to be heard in the name of a prophet, since it was as a prophet that He had to be regarded by the people. “A prophet,” says Moses, “shall the Lord your God raise up unto you, of your sons” (that is, of course, after a carnal descent[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4353]); “unto Him shall ye hearken, as unto me.”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4354] “Every one who will not hearken unto Him, his soul[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4355] shall be cut off from amongst his people.”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4356] So also Isaiah: “Who is there among you that feareth God? Let him hear the voice of His Son.”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4357] This voice the Father was going Himself to recommend. For, says he,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4358] He establishes the words of His Son, when He says, “This is my beloved Son, hear ye Him.” Therefore, even if there be made a transfer of the obedient “hearing” from Moses and Elias to[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4359] Christ, it is still not from another God, or to another Christ; but from[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4360] the Creator to His Christ, in consequence of the departure of the old covenant and the supervening of the new. “Not an ambassador, nor an angel, but He Himself,” says Isaiah, “shall save them;”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4361] for it is He Himself who is now declaring and fulfilling the law and the prophets. The Father gave to the Son new disciples,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4362] after that Moses and Elias had been exhibited along with Him in the honour of His glory, and had then been dismissed as having fully discharged their duty and office, for the express purpose of affirming for Marcion’s information the fact that Moses and Elias had a share in even the glory of Christ. But we have the entire structure[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4363] of this same vision in Habakkuk also, where the Spirit in the person of some[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4364] of the apostles says, “O Lord, I have heard Thy speech, and was afraid.” What speech was this, other than the words of the voice from heaven, This is my beloved Son, hear ye Him? “I considered thy works, and was astonished.” When could this have better happened than when Peter, on seeing His glory, knew not what he was saying? “In the midst of the two Thou shalt be known”—even Moses and Elias.[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4365] These likewise did Zechariah see under the figure of the two olive trees and olive branches.[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4366] For these are they of whom he says, “They are the two anointed ones, that stand by the Lord of the whole earth.” And again Habakkuk says, “His glory covered the heavens” (that is, with that cloud), “and His splendour shall be like the light—even the light, wherewith His very raiment glistened.” And if we would make mention of[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4367] the promise to Moses, we shall find it accomplished here. For when Moses desired to see the Lord, saying, “If therefore I have found grace in Thy sight, manifest Thyself to me, that I may see Thee distinctly,”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4368] the sight which he desired to have was of that condition which he was to assume as man, and which as a prophet he knew was to occur. Respecting the *face* of God, however, he had already heard, “No man shall see me, and live.” “This thing,” said He, “which thou hast spoken, will I do unto thee.” Then Moses said, “Show me Thy glory.” And the Lord, with like reference to the future, replied, “I will pass before thee in my glory,” etc. Then at the last He says, “And then thou shalt see my back.”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4369] Not loins, or calves of the legs, did he want to behold, but the glory which was to be revealed in the latter days.[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4370] He had promised that He would make Himself thus face to face visible to him, when He said to Aaron, “If there shall be a prophet among you, I will make myself known to him by vision, and by vision will I speak with him; but not so is my manner to Moses; with *him* will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently” (that is to say, in the form of man which He was to assume), “and not in dark speeches.”[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4371] Now, although Marcion has denied[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4372] that he is here represented as speaking with the Lord, but only as standing, yet, inasmuch as he stood “mouth to mouth,” he must also have stood “face to face” *with him*, to use his words,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4373] not far from him, in His very glory—not to say,[^the-same-conclusion-supported-by-the-transfiguration-4374] in His presence. And with this glory he went away enlightened from Christ, just as he used to do from the Creator; as *then* to dazzle the eyes of the children of Israel, so *now* to smite those of the blinded Marcion, who has failed to see how this argument also makes against him.

### Impossible that Marcion's Christ Should Reprove the Faithless Generation. Such Loving Consideration for Infants as the True Christ Was Apt to Shew, Also Impossible for the Other. On the Three Different Characters Confronted and Instructed by Christ in Samaria.

Chapter XXIII.—Impossible that Marcion’s Christ Should Reprove the Faithless Generation. Such Loving Consideration for Infants as the True Christ Was Apt to Shew, Also Impossible for the Other. On the Three Different Characters Confronted and Instructed by Christ in Samaria.

I take on myself the character[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4375] of Israel. Let Marcion’s Christ stand forth, and exclaim, “O faithless generation![^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4376] how long shall I be with you? how long shall I suffer you?”[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4377] He will immediately have to submit to this remonstrance from me: “Whoever you are, O stranger,[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4378] first tell us who you are, from whom you come, and what right you have over us. Thus far, all you possess[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4379] belongs to the Creator. Of course, if you come from Him, and are acting for Him, we will bear your reproof. But if you come from some other god, I should wish you to tell us what you have ever committed to us belonging to yourself,[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4380] which it was our duty to believe, seeing that you are upbraiding us with ‘faithlessness,’ who have never yet revealed to us your own self. How long ago[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4381] did you begin to treat with us, that you should be complaining of the delay? On what points have you borne with us, that you should adduce[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4382] your patience? Like Æsop’s ass, you are just come from the well,[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4383] and are filling every place with your braying.” I assume, besides,[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4384] the person of the disciple, against whom he has inveighed:[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4385] “O perverse nation! how long shall I be with you? how long shall I suffer you?” This outburst of his I might, of course, retort upon him most justly in such words as these: “Whoever you are, O stranger, first tell us who you are, from whom you come, what right you have over us. Thus far, I suppose, you belong to the Creator, and so we have followed you, recognising in you all things which are His. Now, if you come from Him, we will bear your reproof. If, however, you are acting for another, prythee tell us what you have ever conferred upon us that is simply your own, which it had become our duty to believe, seeing that you reproach us with ‘faithlessness,’ although up to this moment you show us no credentials. How long since did you begin to plead with us, that you are charging us with delay? Wherein have you borne with us, that you should even boast of your patience? The ass has only just arrived from Æsop’s well, and he is already braying.” Now who would not thus have rebutted the unfairness of the rebuke, if he had supposed its author to belong to him who had had no right as yet to complain? Except that not even He[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4386] would have inveighed against them, if He had not dwelt among them of old in the law and by the prophets, and with mighty deeds and many mercies, and had always experienced them to be “faithless.” But, behold, Christ takes[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4387] infants, and teaches how all ought to be like them, if they ever wish to be greater.[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4388] The Creator, on the contrary,[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4389] let loose bears against children, in order to avenge His prophet Elisha, who had been mocked by them.[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4390] This antithesis is impudent enough, since it throws together[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4391] things so different as infants[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4392] and children,[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4393]—an age still innocent, and one already capable of discretion—able to mock, if not to blaspheme. As therefore God is a just God, He spared not impious children, exacting as He does honour for every time of life, and especially, of course, from youth. And as God is good, He so loves infants as to have blessed the midwives in Egypt, when they protected the infants of the Hebrews[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4394] which were in peril from Pharaoh’s command.[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4395] Christ therefore shares this kindness with the Creator. As indeed for Marcion’s god, who is an enemy to marriage, how can he possibly seem to be a lover of little children, which are simply the issue of marriage? He who hates the seed must needs also detest the fruit. Yea, he ought to be deemed more ruthless than the king of Egypt.[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4396] For whereas Pharaoh forbade infants to be brought up, *he* will not allow them even to be born, depriving them of their ten months’ existence in the womb. And how much more credible it is, that kindness to little children should be attributed to Him who blessed matrimony for the procreation of mankind, and in such benediction included also the promise of connubial fruit itself, the first of which is that of infancy![^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4397] The Creator, at the request of Elias, inflicts the blow[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4398] of fire from heaven in the case of that false prophet (of Baalzebub).[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4399] I recognise herein the severity of the Judge. And I, on the contrary, the severe rebuke[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4400] of Christ on His disciples, when they were for inflicting[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4401] a like visitation on that obscure village of the Samaritans.[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4402] The heretic, too, may discover that this gentleness of Christ was promised by the selfsame severest Judge. “He shall not contend,” says He, “nor shall His voice be heard in the street; a bruised reed shall He not crush, and smoking flax shall He not quench.”[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4403] Being of such a character, He was of course much the less disposed to burn men. For even at that time the Lord said to Elias,[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4404] “He was not in the fire, but in the still small voice.”[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4405] Well, but why does this most humane and merciful God reject the man who offers himself to Him as an inseparable companion?[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4406] If it were from pride or from hypocrisy that he had said, “I will follow Thee whithersoever Thou goest,’ then, by judicially reproving an act of either pride or hypocrisy as worthy of rejection, He performed the office of a Judge. And, of course, him whom He rejected He condemned to the loss of not following the Saviour.[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4407] For as He calls to salvation him whom He does not reject, or him whom He voluntarily invites, so does He consign to perdition him whom He rejects. When, however, He answers the man, who alleged as an excuse his father’s burial, “Let the dead bury their dead, but go thou and preach the kingdom of God,”[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4408] He gave a clear confirmation to those two laws of the Creator—that in Leviticus, which concerns the sacerdotal office, and forbids the priests to be present at the funerals even of their parents. “The priest,” says He, “shall not enter where there is any dead person;[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4409] and for his father he shall not be defiled”[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4410]; as well as that in Numbers, which relates to the (Nazarite) vow of separation; for there he who devotes himself to God, among other things, is bidden “not to come at any dead body,” not even of his father, or his mother, or his brother.[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4411] Now it was, I suppose, for the Nazarite and the priestly office that He intended this man whom He had been inspiring[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4412] to preach the kingdom of God. Or else, if it be not so, he must be pronounced impious enough who, without the intervention of any precept of the law, commanded that burials of parents should be neglected by their sons. When, indeed, in the third case before us, (Christ) forbids the man “to look back” who wanted first “to bid his family farewell,” He only follows out the rule[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4413] of the Creator. For this (retrospection) He had been against their making, whom He had rescued out of Sodom.[^impossible-that-marcion-s-christ-should-reprove-4414]

### On the Mission of the Seventy Disciples, and Christ's Charge to Them. Precedents Drawn from the Old Testament. Absurdity of Supposing that Marcion's Christ Could Have Given the Power of Treading on Serpents and Scorpions.

Chapter XXIV.—On the Mission of the Seventy Disciples, and Christ’s Charge to Them. Precedents Drawn from the Old Testament. Absurdity of Supposing that Marcion’s Christ Could Have Given the Power of Treading on Serpents and Scorpions.

He chose also seventy other missionaries[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4415] besides the twelve. Now why, if the twelve followed the number of the twelve fountains of Elim,[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4416] should not the seventy correspond to the like number of the palms of that place?[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4417] Whatever be the *Antitheses* of the comparison, it is a diversity in the causes, not in the powers, which has mainly produced them. But if one does not keep in view the diversity of the *causes*,[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4418] he is very apt to infer a difference of *powers*.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4419] When the children of Israel went out of Egypt, the Creator brought them forth laden with their spoils of gold and silver vessels, and with loads besides of raiment and unleavened dough;[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4420] whereas Christ commanded His disciples not to carry even a staff[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4421] for their journey. The former were thrust forth into a desert, but the latter were sent into cities. Consider the difference presented in the occasions,[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4422] and you will understand how it was one and the same power which arranged the mission[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4423] of His people according to their poverty in the one case, and their plenty in the other. He cut down[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4424] their supplies when they could be replenished through the cities, just as He had accumulated[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4425] them when exposed to the scantiness of the desert. Even shoes He forbade them to carry. For it was He under whose very protection the people wore not out a shoe,[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4426] even in the wilderness for the space of so many years. “No one,” says He, “shall ye salute by the way.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4427] What a destroyer of the prophets, forsooth, is Christ, seeing it is from them that He received his precept also! When Elisha sent on his servant Gehazi before him to raise the Shunammite’s son from death, I rather think he gave him these instructions:[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4428] “Gird up thy loins, and take my staff in thine hand, and go thy way: if thou meet any man, salute him not;[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4429] and if any salute thee, answer him not again.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4430] For what is a wayside blessing but a mutual salutation as men meet? So also the Lord commands: “Into whatsoever house they enter, let them say, Peace be to it.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4431] Herein He follows the very same example. For Elisha enjoined upon his servant the same salutation when he met the Shunammite; he was to say to her: “Peace to thine husband, peace to thy child.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4432] Such will be rather our *Antitheses*; they compare Christ with, instead of sundering Him from, the Creator. “The labourer is worthy of his hire.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4433] Who could better pronounce such a sentence than the Judge? For to decide that the workman deserves his wages, is in itself a judicial act. There is no award which consists not in a process of judgment. The law of the Creator on this point also presents us with a corroboration, for He judges that labouring oxen are as labourers worthy of their hire: “Thou shalt not muzzle,” says He, “the ox when he treadeth out the corn.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4434] Now, who is so good to man[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4435] as He who is also merciful to cattle? Now, when Christ pronounced labourers to be worthy of their hire, He, in fact, exonerated from blame that precept of the Creator about depriving the Egyptians of their gold and silver vessels.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4436] For they who had built for the Egyptians their houses and cities, were surely workmen worthy of their hire, and were not instructed in a fraudulent act, but only set to claim compensation for their hire, which they were unable in any other way to exact from their masters.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4437] That the kingdom of God was neither new nor unheard of, He in this way affirmed, whilst at the same time He bids them announce that it was near at hand.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4438] Now it is that which was once far off, which can be properly said to have become near. If, however, a thing had never existed previous to its becoming near, it could never have been said to have approached, because it had never existed at a distance. Everything which is new and unknown is also sudden.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4439] Everything which is sudden, then, first receives the accident of time[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4440] when it is announced, for it then first puts on appearance of form.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4441] Besides it will be impossible for a thing either to have been tardy[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4442] all the while it remained unannounced,[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4443] or to have approached[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4444] from the time it shall begin to be announced.

He likewise adds, that they should say to such as would not receive them: “Notwithstanding be ye sure of this, that the kingdom of God is come nigh unto you.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4445] If He does not enjoin this by way of a commination, the injunction is a most useless one. For what mattered it to them that the kingdom was at hand, unless its approach was accompanied with judgment?—even for the salvation of such as received the announcement thereof. How, if there can be a threat without its accomplishment, can you have in a threatening god, one that executes also, and in both, one that is a judicial being?[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4446] So, again, He commands that the dust be shaken off against them, as a testimony,—the very particles of their ground which might cleave[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4447] to the sandal, not to mention[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4448] any other sort of communication with them.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4449] But if their churlishness[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4450] and inhospitality were to receive no vengeance from Him, for what purpose does He premise a testimony, which surely forbodes some threats? Furthermore, when the Creator also, in the book of Deuteronomy, forbids the reception of the Ammonites and the Moabites into the church,[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4451] because, when His people came from Egypt, they fraudulently withheld provisions from them with inhumanity and inhospitality,[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4452] it will be manifest that the prohibition of intercourse descended to Christ from Him. The form of it which He uses—“He that despiseth you, despiseth me”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4453]—the Creator had also addressed to Moses: “Not against thee have they murmured, but against me.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4454] Moses, indeed, was as much an apostle as the apostles were prophets. The authority of both offices will have to be equally divided, as it proceeds from one and the same Lord, (the God) of apostles and prophets. Who is He that shall bestow “the power of treading on serpents and scorpions?”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4455] Shall it be He who is the Lord of all living creatures or he who is not god over a single lizard? Happily the Creator has promised by Isaiah to give this power even to little children, of putting their hand in the cockatrice den and on the hole of the young asps without at all receiving hurt.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4456] And, indeed, we are aware (without doing violence to the literal sense of the passage, since even these noxious animals have actually been unable to do hurt where there has been faith) that under the figure of scorpions and serpents are portended evil spirits, whose very prince is described[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4457] by the name of serpent, dragon, and every other most conspicuous beast in the power of the Creator.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4458] This power the Creator conferred first of all upon His Christ, even as the ninetieth Psalm says to Him: “Upon the asp and the basilisk shalt Thou tread; the lion and the dragon shalt Thou trample under foot.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4459] So also Isaiah: “In that day the Lord God shall draw His sacred, great, and strong sword” (even His Christ) “against that dragon, that great and tortuous serpent; and He shall slay him in that day.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4460] But when the same prophet says, “The way shall be called a clean and holy way; over it the unclean thing shall not pass, nor shall be there any unclean way; but the dispersed shall pass over it, and they shall not err therein; no lion shall be there, nor any ravenous beast shall go up thereon; it shall not be found there,”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4461] he points out the way of faith, by which we shall reach to God; and then to this way of faith he promises this utter crippling[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4462] and subjugation of all noxious animals. Lastly, you may discover the suitable times of the promise, if you read what precedes the passage: “Be strong, ye weak hands and ye feeble knees: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb shall be articulate.”[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4463] When, therefore, He proclaimed the benefits of His cures, then also did He put the scorpions and the serpents under the feet of His saints—even He who had first received this power from the Father, in order to bestow it upon others and then manifested it forth conformably to the order of prophecy.[^on-the-mission-of-the-seventy-disciples-4464]

### Christ Thanks the Father for Revealing to Babes What He Had Concealed from the Wise. This Concealment Judiciously Effected by the Creator. Other Points in St. Luke's Chap. X. Shown to Be Only Possible to the Creator's Christ.

Chapter XXV.—Christ Thanks the Father for Revealing to Babes What He Had Concealed from the Wise. This Concealment Judiciously Effected by the Creator. Other Points in St. Luke’s Chap. X. Shown to Be Only Possible to the Creator’s Christ.

Who shall be invoked as the Lord of heaven, that does not first show Himself[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4465] to have been the maker thereof? For He says, “I thank thee, (O Father,) and own Thee, Lord of heaven, because those things which had been hidden from the wise and prudent, Thou has revealed unto babes.”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4466] What things are these? And whose? And by whom hidden? And by whom revealed? If it was by Marcion’s god that they were hidden and revealed, it was an extremely iniquitous proceeding;[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4467] for nothing at all had he ever produced[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4468] in which anything could have been hidden—no prophecies, no parables, no visions, no evidences[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4469] of things, or words, or names, obscured by allegories and figures, or cloudy enigmas, but he had concealed the greatness even of himself, which he was with all his might revealing by his Christ. Now in what respect had the wise and prudent done wrong,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4470] that God should be hidden from them, when their wisdom and prudence had been insufficient to come to the knowledge of Him? No way had been provided by himself,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4471] by any declaration of his works, or any vestiges whereby they might become[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4472] wise and prudent. However, if they had even failed in any duty towards a god whom they knew not, suppose him now at last to be known still they ought not to have found a jealous god in him who is introduced as unlike the Creator. Therefore, since he had neither provided any materials in which he could have hidden anything, nor had any offenders from whom he could have hidden himself: since, again, even if he had had any, he ought not to have hidden himself from them, he will not now be himself the revealer, who was not previously the concealer; so neither will any be the Lord of heaven nor the Father of Christ but He in whom all these attributes consistently meet.[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4473] For He conceals by His preparatory apparatus of prophetic obscurity, the understanding of which is open to faith (for “if ye will not believe, ye shall not understand”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4474]); and He had offenders in those wise and prudent ones who would not seek after God, although He was to be discovered in His so many and mighty works,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4475] or who rashly philosophized about Him, and thereby furnished to heretics their arts;[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4476] and lastly, He is a jealous God. Accordingly,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4477] that which Christ thanks God for doing, He long ago[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4478] announced by Isaiah: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent will I hide.”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4479] So in another passage He intimates both that He has concealed, and that He will also reveal: “I will give unto them treasures that have been hidden, and secret ones will I discover to them.”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4480] And again: “Who else shall scatter the tokens of ventriloquists,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4481] and the devices of those who divine out of their own heart; turning wise men backward, and making their counsels foolish?”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4482] Now, if He has designated His Christ as an enlightener of the Gentiles, saying, “I have set thee for a light of the Gentiles;”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4483] and if we understand these to be meant in the word *babes*[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4484]—as having been once dwarfs in knowledge and infants in prudence, and even now also babes in their lowliness of faith—we shall of course more easily understand how He who had once hidden “these things,” and promised a revelation of them through Christ, was the same God as He who had now revealed them unto babes. Else, if it was Marcion’s god who revealed the things which had been formerly hidden by the Creator, it follows[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4485] that he did the Creator’s work by setting forth His deeds.[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4486] But he did it, say you, for His destruction, that he might refute them.[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4487] Therefore he ought to have refuted them to those from whom the Creator had hidden them, even the wise and prudent. For if he had a kind intention in what he did, the gift of knowledge was due to those from whom the Creator had detained it, instead of the *babes*, to whom the Creator had grudged no gift. But after all, it is, I presume, the edification[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4488] rather than the demolition[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4489] of the law and the prophets which we have thus far found effected in Christ. “All things,” He says, “are delivered unto me of my Father.”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4490] You may believe Him, if He is the Christ of the Creator to whom all things belong; because the Creator has not delivered to a Son who is less than Himself all things, which He created by[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4491] Him, that is to say, by His Word. If, on the contrary, he is the notorious stranger,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4492] what are the “*all things*” which have been delivered to him by the Father? Are they the Creator’s? Then the things which the Father delivered to the Son are good, and the Creator is therefore good, since all His “things” are good; whereas he[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4493] is no longer good who has invaded another’s good (domains) to deliver it to his son, thus teaching robbery[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4494] of another’s goods. Surely he must be a most mendacious being, who had no other means of enriching his son than by helping himself to another’s property! Or else,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4495] if nothing of the Creator’s has been delivered to him by the Father, by what right[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4496] does he claim for himself (authority over) man? Or again, if man has been delivered to him, and man alone, then man is not “all things.” But Scripture clearly says that a transfer of *all things* has been made to the Son. If, however, you should interpret this “*all*” of the whole human race, that is, *all nations*, then the delivery of even *these* to the Son is within the purpose of the Creator:[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4497] “I will give Thee the heathen for Thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for Thy possession.”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4498] If, indeed, he has some things of his own, the whole of which he might give to his son, along with the *man* of the Creator, then show some one thing of them all, as a sample, that I may believe; lest I should have as much reason not to believe that all things belong to him, of whom I see nothing, as I have ground for believing that even the things which I see not are His, to whom belongs the universe, which I see. But “no man knoweth who the Father is, but the Son; and who the Son is, but the Father, and he to whom the Son will reveal Him.”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4499] And so it was an unknown god that Christ preached! And other heretics, too, prop themselves up by this passage; alleging in opposition to it that the Creator was known to all, both to Israel by familiar intercourse, and to the Gentiles by nature. Well, how is it He Himself testifies that He was not known to Israel? “But Israel doth not know me, and my people doth not consider me;”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4500] nor to the Gentiles: “For, behold,” says He, “of the nations I have no man.”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4501] Therefore He reckoned them “as the drop of a bucket,”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4502] while “Sion He left as a look-out[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4503] in a vineyard.”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4504] See, then, whether there be not here a confirmation of the prophet’s word, when he rebukes that ignorance of man toward God which continued to the days of the Son of man. For it was on this account that he inserted the clause that the Father is known by him to whom the Son has revealed Him, because it was even He who was announced as set by the Father to be a light to the Gentiles, who of course required to be enlightened concerning God, as well as to Israel, even by imparting to it a fuller knowledge of God. Arguments, therefore, will be of no use for belief in the rival god which may be suitable[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4505] for the Creator, because it is only such as are unfit for the Creator which will be able to advance belief in His rival. If you look also into the next words, “Blessed are the eyes which see the things which ye see, for I tell you that prophets have not seen the things which ye see,”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4506] you will find that they follow from the sense above, that no man indeed had come to the knowledge of God as he ought to have done,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4507] since even the prophets had not seen the things which were being seen under Christ. Now if He had not been my Christ, He would not have made any mention of the prophets in this passage. For what was there to wonder at, if they had not seen the things of a god who had been unknown to them, and was only revealed a long time after them? What blessedness, however, could theirs have been, who were then seeing what others were naturally[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4508] unable to see, since it was of things which they had never predicted that they had not obtained the sight;[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4509] if it were not because they might justly[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4510] have seen the things pertaining to their God, which they had even predicted, but which they at the same time[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4511] had not seen? This, however, will be the blessedness of others, even of such as were seeing the things which others had only foretold. We shall by and by show, nay, we have already shown, that in Christ those things were seen which had been foretold, but yet had been hidden from the very prophets who foretold them, in order that they might be hidden also from the wise and the prudent. In the true Gospel, a certain doctor of the law comes to the Lord and asks, “What shall I do to inherit *eternal* life?” In the heretical gospel life only is mentioned, without the attribute *eternal*; so that the lawyer seems to have consulted Christ simply about the life which the Creator in the law promises to prolong,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4512] and the Lord to have therefore answered him according to the law, “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength,”[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4513] since the question was concerning the conditions of *mere* life. But the lawyer of course knew very well in what way the life which the law meant[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4514] was to be obtained, so that his question could have had no relation to the life whose rules he was himself in the habit of teaching. But seeing that even the dead were now raised by Christ, and being himself excited to the hope of an eternal life by these examples of a restored[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4515] one, he would lose no more time in merely looking on (at the wonderful things which had made him) so high in hope.[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4516] He therefore consulted him about the attainment of eternal life. Accordingly, the Lord, being Himself the same,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4517] and introducing no new precept other than that which relates above all others[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4518] to (man’s) entire salvation, even including the present and the future life,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4519] places before him[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4520] the very essence[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4521] of the law—that he should in every possible way love the Lord his God. If, indeed, it were only about a lengthened life, such as is at the Creator’s disposal, that he inquired and Christ answered, and not about the eternal life, which is at the disposal of Marcion’s god, how is he to obtain the eternal one? Surely not in the same manner as the prolonged life. For in proportion to the difference of the reward must be supposed to be also the diversity of the services. Therefore your disciple, Marcion,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4522] will not obtain his eternal life in consequence of loving your God, in the same way as the man who loves the Creator will secure the lengthened life. But how happens it that, if He is to be loved who promises the prolonged life, He is not much more to be loved who offers the eternal life? Therefore both one and the other life will be at the disposal of one and the same Lord; because one and the same discipline is to be followed[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4523] for one and the other life. What the Creator teaches to be loved, that must He necessarily maintain[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4524] also by Christ,[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4525] for that rule holds good here, which prescribes that greater things ought to be believed of Him who has first lesser proofs to show, than of him for whom no preceding smaller presumptions have secured a claim to be believed in things of higher import. It matters not[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4526] then, whether the word *eternal* has been interpolated by us.[^christ-thanks-the-father-for-revealing-to-4527] It is enough for me, that the Christ who invited men to the eternal—not the lengthened—life, when consulted about the temporal life which he was destroying, did not choose to exhort the man rather to that eternal life which he was introducing. Pray, what would the Creator’s Christ have done, if He who had made man for loving the Creator did not belong to the Creator? I suppose He would have said that the Creator was not to be loved!

### From St. Luke's Eleventh Chapter Other Evidence that Christ Comes from the Creator. The Lord's Prayer and Other Words of Christ. The Dumb Spirit and Christ's Discourse on Occasion of the Expulsion. The Exclamation of the Woman in the Crowd.

Chapter XXVI.—From St. Luke’s Eleventh Chapter Other Evidence that Christ Comes from the Creator. The Lord’s Prayer and Other Words of Christ. The Dumb Spirit and Christ’s Discourse on Occasion of the Expulsion. The Exclamation of the Woman in the Crowd.

When in a certain place he had been praying to that Father above,[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4528] looking up with insolent and audacious eyes to the heaven of the Creator, by whom in His rough and cruel nature he might have been crushed with hail and lightning—just as it was by Him contrived that he was (afterwards) attached to a cross[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4529] at Jerusalem—one of his disciples came to him and said, “Master, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.” This he said, forsooth, because he thought that different prayers were required for different gods! Now, he who had advanced such a conjecture as this should first show that another god had been proclaimed by Christ. For nobody would have wanted to know how to pray, before he had learned whom he was to pray to. If, however, he had already learned this, prove it. If you find nowhere any proof, let me tell you[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4530] that it was to the Creator that he asked for instruction in prayer, to whom John’s disciples also used to pray. But, inasmuch as John had introduced some new order of prayer, this disciple had not improperly presumed to think that he ought also to ask of Christ whether they too must not (according to some special rule of their Master) pray, not indeed to another god, but in another manner. Christ accordingly[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4531] would not have taught His disciple prayer before He had given him the knowledge of God Himself. Therefore what He actually taught was prayer to Him whom the disciple had already known. In short, you may discover in the import[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4532] of the prayer what God is addressed therein. To whom can I say, “Father?”[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4533] To him who had nothing to do with making me, from whom I do not derive my origin? Or to Him, who, by making and fashioning me, became my parent?[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4534] Of whom can I ask for His Holy Spirit? Of him who gives not even the mundane spirit;[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4535] or of Him “who maketh His angels spirits,” and whose Spirit it was which in the beginning hovered upon the waters.[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4536] Whose kingdom shall I wish to come—his, of whom I never heard as the king of glory; or His, in whose hand are even the hearts of kings? Who shall give me my daily[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4537] bread? Shall it be he who produces for me not a grain of millet-seed;[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4538] or He who even from heaven gave to His people day by day the bread of angels?[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4539] Who shall forgive me my trespasses?[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4540] He who, by refusing to judge them, does not retain them; or He who, unless He forgives them, will retain them, even to His judgment? Who shall suffer us not to be led into temptation? He before whom the tempter will never be able to tremble; or He who from the beginning has beforehand condemned[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4541] the angel tempter? If any one, with such a form,[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4542] invokes another god and not the Creator, he does not pray; he only blasphemes.[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4543] In like manner, from whom must I ask that I may receive? Of whom seek, that I may find? To whom knock, that it may be opened to me?[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4544] Who has to give to him that asks, but He to whom all things belong, and whose am I also that am the asker? What, however, have I lost before that other god, that I should seek of him and find it. If it be wisdom and prudence, it is the Creator who has hidden them. Shall I resort to him, then, in quest of them? If it be health[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4545] and life, they are at the disposal of the Creator. Nor must anything be sought and found anywhere else than there, where it is kept in secret that it may come to light. So, again, at no other door will I knock than at that out of which my privilege has reached me.[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4546] In fine, if to receive, and to find, and to be admitted, is the fruit of labour and earnestness to him who has asked, and sought, and knocked, understand that these duties have been enjoined, and results promised, by the Creator. As for that most excellent god of yours, coming as he professes gratuitously to help man, who was not his (creature),[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4547] he could not have imposed upon him any labour, or (endowed him with) any earnestness. For he would by this time cease to be the most excellent god, were he not spontaneously to give to every one who does not ask, and permit every one who seeks not to find, and open to every one who does not knock. The Creator, on the contrary,[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4548] was able to proclaim these duties and rewards by Christ, in order that man, who by sinning had offended his God, might toil on (in his probation), and by his perseverance in asking might receive, and in seeking might find, and in knocking might enter. Accordingly, the preceding similitude[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4549] represents the man who went at night and begged for the loaves, in the light of a friend and not a stranger, and makes him knock at a friend’s house and not at a stranger’s. But even if he has offended, man is more of a friend with the Creator than with the god of Marcion. At His door, therefore, does he knock to whom he had the right of access; whose gate he had found; whom he knew to possess bread; in bed now with His children, whom He had willed to be born.[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4550] Even though the knocking is late in the day, it is yet the Creator’s time. To Him belongs the latest hour who owns an entire age[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4551] and the end thereof. As for the new god, however, no one could have knocked at his door late, for he has hardly yet[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4552] seen the light of morning. It is the Creator, who once shut the door to the Gentiles, which was then knocked at by the Jews, that both rises and gives, if not now to man as a friend, yet not as a stranger, but, as He says, “because of his importunity.”[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4553] *Importunate*, however, the recent god could not have permitted any one to be in the short time (since his appearance).[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4554] Him, therefore, whom you call the Creator recognise also as “Father.” It is even He who knows what His children require. For when they asked for bread, He gave them manna from heaven; and when they wanted flesh, He sent them abundance of quails—not a serpent for a fish, nor for an egg a scorpion.[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4555] It will, however, appertain to Him not to give evil instead of good, who has both one and the other in His power. Marcion’s god, on the contrary, not having a scorpion, was unable to refuse to give what he did not possess; only He (could do so), who, having a scorpion, yet gives it not. In like manner, it is He who will give the Holy Spirit, at whose command[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4556] is also the unholy spirit. When He cast out the “demon which was dumb”[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4557] (and by a cure of this sort verified Isaiah),[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4558] and having been charged with casting out demons by Beelzebub, He said, “If I by Beelzebub cast out demons, by whom do your sons cast them out?”[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4559] By such a question what does He otherwise mean, than that He ejects the spirits by the same power by which their sons also did—that is, by the power of the Creator? For if you suppose the meaning to be, “If I by Beelzebub, etc., by whom your sons?”—as if He would reproach them with having the power of Beelzebub,—you are met at once by the preceding sentence, that “Satan cannot be divided against himself.”[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4560] So that it was not by Beelzebub that even they were casting out demons, but (as we have said) by the power of the Creator; and that He might make this understood, He adds: “But if I with the finger of God cast out demons, is not the kingdom of God come near unto you?”[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4561] For the magicians who stood before Pharaoh and resisted Moses called the power of the Creator “*the finger of God*.”[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4562] It was the finger of God, because it was a sign[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4563] that even a thing of weakness was yet abundant in strength. This Christ also showed, when, recalling to notice (and not obliterating) those ancient wonders which were really His own,[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4564] He said that the power of God must be understood to be the finger of none other God than Him, under[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4565] whom it had received this appellation. *His* kingdom, therefore, was come near to them, whose power was called His “finger.” Well, therefore, did He connect[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4566] with the parable of “the strong man armed,” whom “a stronger man still overcame,”[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4567] the prince of the demons, whom He had already called Beelzebub and Satan; signifying that it was he who was overcome by the finger of God, and not that the Creator had been subdued by another god. Besides,[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4568] how could His kingdom be still standing, with its boundaries, and laws, and functions, whom, even if the whole world were left entire to Him, Marcion’s god could possibly seem to have overcome as “the stronger than He,” if it were not in consequence of His law that even Marcionites were constantly dying, by returning in their dissolution[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4569] to the ground, and were so often admonished by even a scorpion, that the Creator had by no means been overcome?[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4570] “A (certain) mother of the company exclaims, ‘Blessed is the womb that bare Thee, and the paps which Thou hast sucked;’ but the Lord said, ‘Yea, rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.’”[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4571] Now He had in precisely similar terms rejected His mother or His brethren, whilst preferring those who heard and obeyed God.[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4572] His mother, however, was not here present with Him. On that former occasion, therefore, He had not denied that He was her son by birth.[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4573] On hearing this (salutation) the second time, He the second time transferred, as He had done before,[^from-st-luke-s-eleventh-chapter-other-4574] the “blessedness” to His disciples from the womb and the paps of His mother, from whom, however, unless He had in her (a real mother) He could not have transferred it.

### Christ's Reprehension of the Pharisees Seeking a Sign. His Censure of Their Love of Outward Show Rather Than Inward Holiness. Scripture Abounds with Admonitions of a Similar Purport. Proofs of His Mission from the Creator.

Chapter XXVII.—Christ’s Reprehension of the Pharisees Seeking a Sign. His Censure of Their Love of Outward Show Rather Than Inward Holiness. Scripture Abounds with Admonitions of a Similar Purport. Proofs of His Mission from the Creator.

I prefer elsewhere refuting[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4575] the faults which the Marcionites find in the Creator. It is here enough that they are also found in Christ.[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4576] Behold how unequal, inconsistent, and capricious he is! Teaching one thing and doing another, he enjoins “giving to every one that seeks;” and yet he himself refuses to give to those “who seek a sign.”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4577] For a vast age he hides his own light from men, and yet says that a candle must not be hidden, but affirms that it ought to be set upon a candlestick, that it may give light to all.[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4578] He forbids cursing *again*, and cursing much more of course; and yet he heaps his *woe* upon the Pharisees and doctors of the law.[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4579] Who so closely resembles my God as His own Christ? We have often already laid it down for certain,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4580] that He could not have been branded[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4581] as the destroyer of the law if He had promulged another god. Therefore even the Pharisee, who invited Him to dinner in the passage before us,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4582] expressed some surprise[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4583] in His presence that He had not washed before He sat down to meat, in accordance with the law, since it was the God of the law that He was proclaiming.[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4584] Jesus also interpreted the law to him when He told him that they “made clean the outside of the cup and the platter, whereas their inward part was full of ravening and wickedness.” *This He said*, to signify that by the cleansing of vessels was to be understood before God the purification of men, inasmuch as it was about a man, and not about an unwashed vessel, that even this Pharisee had been treating in His presence. He therefore said: “You wash the outside of the cup,” that is, the flesh, “but you do not cleanse your inside part,”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4585] that is, the soul; adding: “Did not He that made the outside,” that is, the flesh, “also make the inward part,” that is to say, the soul?—by which assertion He expressly declared that to the same God belongs the cleansing of a man’s external and internal nature, both alike being in the power of Him who prefers mercy not only to man’s washing,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4586] but even to sacrifice.[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4587] For He subjoins the command: “Give what ye possess as alms, and all things shall be clean unto you.”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4588] Even if another god could have enjoined mercy, he could not have done so previous to his becoming known. Furthermore, it is in this passage evident that they[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4589] were not reproved concerning their God, but concerning a point of His instruction to them, when He prescribed to them figuratively the cleansing of their vessels, but really the works of merciful dispositions. In like manner, He upbraids them for tithing paltry herbs,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4590] but at the same time “passing over hospitality[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4591] and the love of God.”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4592] The vocation and the love of what God, but Him by whose law of tithes they used to offer their rue and mint? For the whole point of the rebuke lay in this, that they cared about small matters in His service of course, to whom they failed to exhibit their weightier duties when He commanded them: “Thou shalt love with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, the Lord thy God, who hath called thee out of Egypt.”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4593] Besides, time enough had not yet passed to admit of Christ’s requiring so premature—nay, as yet so distasteful[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4594]—a love towards a new and recent, not to say a hardly yet developed,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4595] deity. When, again, He upbraids those who caught at the uppermost places and the honour of public salutations, He only follows out the Creator’s course,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4596] who calls ambitious persons of this character “rulers of Sodom,”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4597] who forbids us “to put confidence even in princes,”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4598] and pronounces him to be altogether wretched who places his confidence in man. But whoever[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4599] aims at high position, because he would glory in the officious attentions[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4600] of other people, (in every such case,) inasmuch as He forbade such attentions (in the shape) of placing hope and confidence in man, He at the same time[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4601] censured all who were ambitious of high positions. He also inveighs against the doctors of the law themselves, because they were “lading men with burdens grievous to be borne, which they did not venture to touch with even a finger of their own;”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4602] but not as if He made a mock of[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4603] the burdens of the law with any feeling of detestation towards it. For how could He have felt aversion to the law, who used with so much earnestness to upbraid them for passing over its weightier matters, alms—giving, hospitality,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4604] and the love of God? Nor, indeed, was it only these great things (which He recognized), but even[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4605] the tithes of rue and the cleansing of cups. But, in truth, He would rather have deemed them excusable for being unable to carry burdens which could not be borne. What, then, are the burdens which He censures?[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4606] None but those which they were accumulating of their own accord, when they taught for commandments the doctrines of men; for the sake of private advantage joining house to house, so as to deprive their neighbour of his own; cajoling[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4607] the people, loving gifts, pursuing rewards, robbing the poor of the rights of judgment, that they might have the widow for a prey and the fatherless for a spoil.[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4608] Of these Isaiah also says, “Woe unto them that are strong in Jerusalem!”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4609] and again, “They that demand you shall rule over you.”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4610] And who did this more than the lawyers?[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4611] Now, if these offended Christ, it was as belonging to Him that they offended Him. He would have aimed no blow at the teachers of an alien law. But why is a “woe” pronounced against them for “building the sepulchres of the prophets whom their fathers had killed?”[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4612] They rather deserved praise, because by such an act of piety they seemed to show that they did not allow the deeds of their fathers. Was it not because (Christ) was jealous[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4613] of such a disposition as the Marcionites denounce,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4614] visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the fourth generation? What “key,” indeed, was it which these lawyers had,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4615] but the interpretation of the law? Into the perception of this they neither entered themselves, even because they did not believe (for “unless ye believe, ye shall not understand”); nor did they permit others to enter, because they preferred to teach them for commandments even the doctrines of men. When, therefore, He reproached those who did not themselves enter in, and also shut the door against others, must He be regarded as a disparager of the law, or as a supporter of it? If a disparager, those who were hindering the law ought to have been pleased; if a supporter, He is no longer an enemy of the law.[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4616] But all these imprecations He uttered in order to tarnish the Creator as a cruel Being,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4617] against whom such as offended were destined to have a “woe.” And who would not rather have feared to provoke a cruel Being,[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4618] by withdrawing allegiance[^christ-s-reprehension-of-the-pharisees-seeking-4619] from Him? Therefore the more He represented the Creator to be an object of fear, the more earnestly would He teach that He ought to be served. Thus would it behove the Creator’s Christ to act.
